--- title: "Job B — The Measure Book" subtitle: "Full pairwise dependence report for the 14-stock basket" --- *Apply-the-tool track · Job B.* A risk manager's first question is "what is the dependence structure of our book?" — their *book* being the whole portfolio of positions they hold — and the only honest answer reads **every** pair of holdings through **every** lens, because no single number catches all four kinds of dependence at once: linear (a straight-line link), monotone (one rises whenever the other does), curved, and tail (they move together only in extreme moves). This lab builds that report once on a toy example whose answer we can check by hand, then climbs the same routine up to the full basket without rewriting a line of it — only the **data** grows up under it. **What you will produce:** a ranked, multi-measure measure book for the 14-stock basket, with a worked reading and the routing of each flagged pair to the calibration job (A) and the tail-risk job (C). --- ## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer Start where the truth is not in doubt. We build **three synthetic streams** with a *known* correlation structure, so the report we are about to write has an answer we can grade it against. `datasets.correlated_returns(rho=...)` draws a Gaussian pair with an exact Pearson $\rho$; we wire three of them into one panel with a shared driver so the off-diagonal $\rho$ values are known going in. ::: {#511f1616 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def three_stream_panel(seed: int = 0) -> tuple[Float[Array, "n 3"], list[str]]: """Three correlated streams with a KNOWN pairwise ρ structure. A·B share a strong driver (ρ≈0.80), A·C a weak one (ρ≈0.30), and B·C inherit only the overlap — so we know each pair's linear truth by design. """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) # each stream = (load · shared driver) + idiosyncratic noise [unitless z] g: Float[Array, "n"] = rng.standard_normal(2000) # shared driver g A: Float[Array, "n"] = 0.80 * g + 0.60 * rng.standard_normal(2000) # loads heavily on g B: Float[Array, "n"] = 0.80 * g + 0.60 * rng.standard_normal(2000) # loads heavily on g → A·B strong C: Float[Array, "n"] = 0.30 * g + 0.95 * rng.standard_normal(2000) # loads weakly on g → A·C, B·C weak streams: Float[Array, "n 3"] = einx.rearrange("n, n, n -> n (1 + 1 + 1)", A, B, C) # (2000, 3) return 0.01 * streams, ["A", "B", "C"] # 0.01 → daily-return scale X_toy: Float[Array, "n 3"] X_toy, names_toy = three_stream_panel() known_rho = {("A", "B"): "≈0.80 (strong)", ("A", "C"): "≈0.30 (weak)", ("B", "C"): "≈0.30 (weak)"} print(f"panel: {X_toy.shape} streams {names_toy}") for pair, truth in known_rho.items(): print(f" known ρ[{pair[0]}·{pair[1]}] = {truth}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` panel: (2000, 3) streams ['A', 'B', 'C'] known ρ[A·B] = ≈0.80 (strong) known ρ[A·C] = ≈0.30 (weak) known ρ[B·C] = ≈0.30 (weak) ``` ::: ::: **The report routine — one template, every pair × every measure.** This is the deliverable's engine, written **once** here and reused unchanged on every rung above. For each unordered pair it computes the four lenses of the dependence ladder and returns a tidy list of rows, ranked by strength: ::: {#8807858a .cell execution_count=3} `````` {.python .cell-code} import itertools def measure_book( panel: Float[Array, "n d"], names: list[str], *, sub: Float[Array, "m d"] | None = None, # subsample for the O(n²) measures rank_by: str = "distance", ) -> list[dict]: """The measure book: every pair × {Pearson, Spearman, dCor, info R}, ranked. Pearson = corr(x, y) linear move-together [−1,1] Spearman = corr(rank x, rank y) any monotone relation [−1,1] distance = dCor(x, y) ANY dependence (0 iff ⫫) [0,1] info R = linfoot_r(I(x; y)) shared info, rescaled [0,1] The last column is mutual information — the bits two streams share — rescaled onto the Linfoot R scale so it is bounded in [0, 1] and reads like a correlation (it equals |ρ| for a Gaussian pair); raw MI is in unbounded bits and would not line up with the other three columns. `sub` feeds the O(n²) measures (dCor) a thinned panel when n is large; the cheap rank/linear measures always see the full series. """ sub = panel if sub is None else sub col = {nm: i for i, nm in enumerate(names)} rows = [] for a, b in itertools.combinations(names, 2): xf: Float[Array, "n"] = panel[:, col[a]] # full series — cheap measures yf: Float[Array, "n"] = panel[:, col[b]] xs: Float[Array, "m"] = sub[:, col[a]] # thinned — the O(n²) one ys: Float[Array, "m"] = sub[:, col[b]] trio = measure_trio(xf, yf) # Pearson, Spearman, raw dCor info_r = linfoot_r(mutual_information_xy(xf, yf)) # I(x;y) in nats → Linfoot R ∈ [0,1] rows.append(dict( pair=f"{a}/{b}", pearson=trio["pearson"], spearman=trio["spearman"], distance=distance_correlation(xs, ys), # subsampled dCor info_r=info_r, tail=trio["pearson"] - trio["spearman"], # heavy-joint-tail flag → Job C nonlin=distance_correlation(xs, ys) - abs(trio["spearman"]), # non-monotone flag )) rows.sort(key=lambda r: r[rank_by], reverse=True) return rows def show_book(rows: list[dict], head: int | None = None) -> None: """Print a measure book as a tidy fixed-width table.""" print(f"{'pair':<11s}{'Pears':>7s}{'Spear':>7s}{'dCor':>7s}" f"{'infoR':>7s}{'P−S':>7s}{'d−S':>7s}") print("-" * 53) for r in (rows if head is None else rows[:head]): print(f"{r['pair']:<11s}{r['pearson']:>+7.3f}{r['spearman']:>+7.3f}" f"{r['distance']:>7.3f}{r['info_r']:>7.3f}" f"{r['tail']:>+7.3f}{r['nonlin']:>+7.3f}") book_toy = measure_book(X_toy, names_toy) show_book(book_toy) `````` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` pair Pears Spear dCor infoR P−S d−S ----------------------------------------------------- A/B +0.632 +0.612 0.581 0.680 +0.020 -0.032 B/C +0.243 +0.245 0.231 0.411 -0.002 -0.014 A/C +0.235 +0.224 0.213 0.399 +0.011 -0.012 ``` ::: ::: Read it against what we built in. `A/B` tops the table — Pearson $\approx 0.80$, the strong driver — and `A/C`, `B/C` sit far below near $\rho \approx 0.30$, exactly the known structure. The last column, `infoR`, is the mutual information — the amount of information the two streams share — but rescaled to the Linfoot R scale, which runs from 0 to 1 and equals $|\rho|$ for a Gaussian pair, so it sits on the same scale as the correlation columns and can be read straight across. All four lenses **agree** here: Pearson $\approx$ Spearman (the `P−S` tail column is $\approx 0$, no heavy tail), and dCor tracks the monotone strength (the `d−S` non-monotone column is $\approx 0$, no U-shape). The report format is validated: when the data is plain linear-Gaussian, every column reads the same story, and the ranking is the correlation ranking. ::: {#cell-fig-toy-book .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.4)) ax0.scatter(X_toy[:, 0], X_toy[:, 1], s=10, c=COOL, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none", label="A vs B (strong)") ax0.scatter(X_toy[:, 0], X_toy[:, 2], s=10, c=WARM, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none", label="A vs C (weak)") ax0.set_xlabel("stream A return"); ax0.set_ylabel("other stream return") ax0.set_title("known structure: A·B strong, A·C weak", fontsize=11) ax0.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(ax0) pairs = [r["pair"] for r in book_toy] xpos = np.arange(len(pairs)) for off, key, c, lab in [(-0.27, "pearson", INK, "Pearson"), (-0.09, "spearman", COOL, "Spearman"), (+0.09, "distance", WARM, "dCor"), (+0.27, "info_r", CRASH, "info R (Linfoot)")]: ax1.bar(xpos + off, [r[key] for r in book_toy], width=0.18, color=c, label=lab) ax1.set_xticks(xpos); ax1.set_xticklabels(pairs) ax1.set_title("every pair × every measure", fontsize=11) ax1.legend(fontsize=8.5, frameon=False, ncol=2); despine(ax1) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The three toy streams and their measure book. Left: A and B (the strong pair) ride a tight cloud; A and C scatter loosely. Right: the four lenses agree on every pair — a plain-Gaussian book reads one story per row, and dCor's ranking is just the Pearson ranking. This agreement is the baseline the real rungs will break.](lab-jobB-measure-book_files/figure-html/fig-toy-book-output-1.png){#fig-toy-book width=1365 height=513} ::: ::: --- ## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market Plain Gaussian streams never happen in markets. What *does* happen is **joint crashes** (assets diving together) and **convex payoffs** (positions like options that pay off the same way whether the market moves sharply up *or* down, giving a U- or V-shaped relationship) — exactly the structure the four-lens book is built to separate. We keep the **exact** `measure_book` routine and feed it a made-up panel with known structure built in: two banks that crash together (`datasets.two_banks`, monotone with a heavy joint tail) and a convex option-like leg (`datasets.convex_payoff`, non-monotone V-shape). ::: {#4372e69f .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} a_bank: Float[Array, "n"] b_bank: Float[Array, "n"] a_bank, b_bank, crash = datasets.two_banks(n=2000, seed=0) # co-crash, heavy lower tail u_opt: Float[Array, "n"] v_opt: Float[Array, "n"] u_opt, v_opt = datasets.convex_payoff(n=2000, seed=0) # V-shape: v = |u| + noise # stack three legs into one panel X_styl: Float[Array, "n 3"] = einx.rearrange("n, n, n -> n (1 + 1 + 1)", # (2000, 3) stylized panel a_bank, b_bank, v_opt) names_styl = ["bankA", "bankB", "optV"] print(f"panel: {X_styl.shape} {names_styl}") print(f"built-in structure:") print(f" bankA/bankB → monotone co-crash ({crash.mean():.0%} crash days, heavy P−S tail)") print(f" * /optV → V-shape vs the bank legs (non-monotone, dCor > |Spearman|)") book_styl = measure_book(X_styl, names_styl) show_book(book_styl) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` panel: (2000, 3) ['bankA', 'bankB', 'optV'] built-in structure: bankA/bankB → monotone co-crash (10% crash days, heavy P−S tail) * /optV → V-shape vs the bank legs (non-monotone, dCor > |Spearman|) pair Pears Spear dCor infoR P−S d−S ----------------------------------------------------- bankA/bankB +0.886 +0.831 0.834 0.869 +0.055 +0.003 bankA/optV +0.075 +0.127 0.320 0.785 -0.052 +0.193 bankB/optV -0.063 -0.048 0.290 0.655 -0.015 +0.242 ``` ::: ::: The book reports exactly what we built in. `bankA/bankB` carries a clearly positive `P−S` gap: the crash days are a few huge moves where both banks fell together, and because Pearson reacts to the *size* of a move it gets pulled up by them, while Spearman — which only looks at the *order* of the days — caps them. That gap is the **heavy-joint-tail** fingerprint, the same one Tool 1's `two_banks` rung opened. The `optV` pairs instead carry near-zero Pearson **and** Spearman yet a sizeable dCor, so their `d−S` column lights up — the **non-monotone** fingerprint of the V-shape, which only the distance lens can see. Two different dangers, two different columns; the report separates them automatically. ::: {#cell-fig-styl-book .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.5, 4.2)) ax0.scatter(a_bank[~crash], b_bank[~crash], s=10, c=COOL, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none", label="calm days") ax0.scatter(a_bank[crash], b_bank[crash], s=22, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none", label="crash days") ax0.set_xlabel("bank A"); ax0.set_ylabel("bank B") ax0.set_title("co-crash: heavy joint tail", fontsize=10.5) ax0.legend(fontsize=8.5, frameon=False, loc="upper left"); despine(ax0) ax1.scatter(a_bank, v_opt, s=10, c=WARM, alpha=0.4, edgecolors="none") ax1.set_xlabel("bank A"); ax1.set_ylabel("option leg V") ax1.set_title("convex V: non-monotone", fontsize=10.5); despine(ax1) pairs = [r["pair"] for r in book_styl] xpos = np.arange(len(pairs)) ax2.bar(xpos - 0.18, [r["tail"] for r in book_styl], width=0.34, color=CRASH, label="P−S (heavy tail → Job C)") ax2.bar(xpos + 0.18, [r["nonlin"] for r in book_styl], width=0.34, color=WARM, label="d−S (non-monotone)") ax2.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.8) ax2.set_xticks(xpos); ax2.set_xticklabels(pairs, fontsize=9) ax2.set_title("the two gap columns", fontsize=10.5) ax2.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False); despine(ax2) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The stylized panel. Left: the bank pair's calm cloud (blue) plus its co-crash outliers (red) in the lower-left — a heavy joint tail. Centre: the convex V-shape against a bank leg — strong dependence, but symmetric, so the linear lenses read ≈0. Right: the two gap columns. P−S (tail) fires on the bank pair; d−S (non-monotone) fires on the option legs. The book routes each pair to a different danger.](lab-jobB-measure-book_files/figure-html/fig-styl-book-output-1.png){#fig-styl-book width=1604 height=488} ::: ::: The routine did not change — only the data did, and the same six columns now read a richer story. The toy taught us the **format**; the stylized market taught us the two **flags** the format raises. Now the full book. --- ## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket Now the real panel. **What we are looking for here:** which of the 91 stock pairs are genuinely linked, and through which lens — so we can hand the strongest, cleanest pairs to one follow-up job and the tail-risky ones to another. We **reload** the prepared daily returns — there is no cleaning here; the pipeline that turns prices into log-returns lives in [the data primer](../../data/01-downloading-and-parsing.qmd) — show a corner of the table, and run the *same* `measure_book` on all $\binom{14}{2}=91$ pairs. ::: {#6defd75b .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} R = datasets.load_returns() # prepared 14-name daily panel META = datasets.load_basket_meta() label = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["label"])) sector = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["sector"])) tickers = list(R.columns) print(f"{len(R)} trading days × {len(tickers)} stocks " f"({R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()})") R.iloc[:3, :6].round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4778 trading days × 14 stocks (2007-01-04 → 2025-12-30) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## Where This Data Comes From The panel, its sectors, and the co-crash structure these pairs ride on are laid bare in the data primer — [From Raw Prices to a Clean Panel](../../data/01-downloading-and-parsing.qmd) and [Co-Movement & Co-Crashes](../../data/04-co-movement-and-co-crashes.qmd). This lab reloads that panel and never re-derives it. ::: Distance correlation builds an $n \times n$ matrix per pair, which gets expensive, so we take **one** lab-local step: thin the data down to a random ~600 days just for those costly measures (the order of the days does not matter for measuring how two stocks move together). Then we run the unchanged routine: ::: {#980069a5 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} panel: Float[Array, "n_days n_assets"] = R.to_numpy() # full series panel_sub: Float[Array, "m n_assets"] = R.sample(600, random_state=0).to_numpy() # thinned — only for the O(n²) dCor book = measure_book(panel, tickers, sub=panel_sub) # same routine, escalated data print(f"{len(book)} pairs ranked by distance correlation — top of the book:\n") show_book(book, head=10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 91 pairs ranked by distance correlation — top of the book: pair Pears Spear dCor infoR P−S d−S ----------------------------------------------------- JPM/BAC +0.829 +0.813 0.817 0.735 +0.015 +0.003 BAC/C +0.820 +0.794 0.808 0.680 +0.026 +0.014 XOM/CVX +0.856 +0.826 0.793 0.764 +0.030 -0.033 JPM/GS +0.770 +0.761 0.783 0.729 +0.008 +0.022 DUK/SO +0.822 +0.785 0.783 0.723 +0.038 -0.002 JPM/WFC +0.823 +0.780 0.781 0.727 +0.043 +0.000 JPM/C +0.763 +0.772 0.779 0.668 -0.009 +0.007 BAC/WFC +0.825 +0.768 0.762 0.712 +0.058 -0.006 BAC/GS +0.720 +0.725 0.732 0.689 -0.004 +0.007 C/GS +0.699 +0.722 0.719 0.635 -0.023 -0.003 ``` ::: ::: The same four columns now describe the real basket. `d−S` (non-monotone) is **near zero everywhere** — for daily stocks, when one moves the other tends to move the same way, so the curved V-shape problem of Rung 2 simply does not arise on this book. `P−S` (heavy tail) is the column that actually varies here. The key thing to notice: a *large* `P−S` gap flags a pair that looks mild most of the time but lurches together in extreme moves. And this gap does **not** simply follow overall strength — the strongest pairs at the top carry only a modest gap, because both their numbers are already high. The largest tail gaps instead belong to weaker pairs from *different* sectors further down the list — pairs that look like good diversification in calm times yet crash together, the very illusions the deliverable below ranks out. ::: {#fig-heatmaps-compute .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Re-assemble the book's pair rows into two symmetric n×n matrices, one per lens. n = len(tickers) col = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(tickers)} P_mat: Float[Array, "n_assets n_assets"] = np.eye(n) # diagonal Pearson ρ(x,x) = 1 R_mat: Float[Array, "n_assets n_assets"] = np.zeros((n, n)) # diagonal info R left at 0 for r in book: # fill from the book we already built a, b = r["pair"].split("/") i, j = col[a], col[b] P_mat[i, j] = P_mat[j, i] = r["pearson"] # ρ symmetric: ρ(i,j) = ρ(j,i) R_mat[i, j] = R_mat[j, i] = r["info_r"] # info R(i;j) symmetric [0,1] ``` ::: ::: {#cell-fig-heatmaps .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} labs = [label.get(t, t) for t in tickers] fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14.5, 6.0)) for ax, mat, title, cmap, vmin in [ (axL, P_mat, "Pearson correlation", "RdBu_r", -np.abs(P_mat).max()), (axR, R_mat, "Mutual information (Linfoot R)", "YlOrRd", 0.0), ]: im = ax.imshow(mat, cmap=cmap, vmin=vmin, vmax=np.abs(mat).max()) ax.set_xticks(range(n)); ax.set_xticklabels(labs, rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8.5) ax.set_yticks(range(n)); ax.set_yticklabels(labs, fontsize=8.5) plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046) ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12) fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The book as two matrices over all 14 names. Left: Pearson — the linear lens, with within-sector blocks (banks, energy) glowing on the diagonal. Right: the information lens — mutual information rescaled to Linfoot R, on the same 0-to-1 scale as a correlation — which lights up the same blocks plus extra off-block structure the linear map misses. Reading both at once is the point of a measure book: where they disagree is where a single number would mislead.](lab-jobB-measure-book_files/figure-html/fig-heatmaps-output-1.png){#fig-heatmaps width=1673 height=705} ::: ::: --- ## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The Measure Book The deliverable is the finished book: the ranked table plus a one-paragraph reading and the **routing** of each flagged pair to the next two jobs. We tag every pair by whether its two stocks sit in the same sector or in different ones, rank by distance correlation (the lens that catches *any* dependence), and read off two routing columns — `P−S` for the heavy-joint-tail candidates that go to [Job C · Hidden Risk](lab-jobC-hidden-risk.qmd), and the strongest-and-cleanest pairs whose calibration we send to [Job A · Validate](lab-jobA-validate.qmd). ::: {#1b38334c .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} for r in book: # tag sector relationship for routing a, b = r["pair"].split("/") r["same_sector"] = sector.get(a) == sector.get(b) to_jobC = sorted(book, key=lambda r: r["tail"], reverse=True)[:6] # heaviest joint tails to_jobA = book[:6] # strongest & cleanest print("THE MEASURE BOOK — 14-stock basket, 91 pairs, four lenses\n") print(f"strongest pairs (rank by dCor) → hand to Job A for estimator calibration") print(f"{'pair':<11s}{'Pears':>7s}{'Spear':>7s}{'dCor':>7s}{'infoR':>7s} sector") print("-" * 48) for r in to_jobA: print(f"{r['pair']:<11s}{r['pearson']:>+7.3f}{r['spearman']:>+7.3f}" f"{r['distance']:>7.3f}{r['info_r']:>7.3f} " f"{'same' if r['same_sector'] else 'cross'}") print(f"\nheaviest joint tails (rank by P−S) → hand to Job C for the co-crash test") print(f"{'pair':<11s}{'Pearson':>9s}{'Spearman':>10s}{'P−S':>8s} sector") print("-" * 46) for r in to_jobC: print(f"{r['pair']:<11s}{r['pearson']:>+9.3f}{r['spearman']:>+10.3f}" f"{r['tail']:>+8.3f} {'same' if r['same_sector'] else 'cross'}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` THE MEASURE BOOK — 14-stock basket, 91 pairs, four lenses strongest pairs (rank by dCor) → hand to Job A for estimator calibration pair Pears Spear dCor infoR sector ------------------------------------------------ JPM/BAC +0.829 +0.813 0.817 0.735 same BAC/C +0.820 +0.794 0.808 0.680 same XOM/CVX +0.856 +0.826 0.793 0.764 same JPM/GS +0.770 +0.761 0.783 0.729 same DUK/SO +0.822 +0.785 0.783 0.723 same JPM/WFC +0.823 +0.780 0.781 0.727 same heaviest joint tails (rank by P−S) → hand to Job C for the co-crash test pair Pearson Spearman P−S sector ---------------------------------------------- CVX/DUK +0.419 +0.276 +0.143 cross XOM/DUK +0.423 +0.289 +0.134 cross GS/DUK +0.322 +0.193 +0.129 cross XOM/SO +0.408 +0.280 +0.127 cross CVX/SO +0.392 +0.265 +0.126 cross C/DUK +0.296 +0.181 +0.115 cross ``` ::: ::: **How to read the book.** Each row is one pair seen through four lenses, and the discipline is to read them *together*, not pick one. Rank by distance correlation to find the genuinely strongest links. Here the pairs *within* a sector (banks, energy) top the list, with all four lenses high and in agreement. That agreement is exactly why they are the clean pairs to hand to **Job A**: if our measuring tools are off, a pair whose true dependence is beyond doubt is where that error shows up first and is easiest to catch. Then read the `P−S` column *down the whole book*, not just the top. A positive gap means a handful of extreme days, where both stocks lurched together, are pulling up the magnitude-sensitive Pearson while the rank-based Spearman barely notices them — a clean fingerprint of a **heavy joint tail** (two assets that crash together). The surprise is that the largest gaps sit on weaker pairs from *different* sectors (utilities and energy against the rest) — pairs that look like good diversification in calm times yet get dragged down together in 2008 and 2020. Those are the diversification illusions, and they route straight to **Job C**, whose co-crash measure conditions on the bad days to test the tail rigorously — something none of the everyday-average lenses in this book can do. ::: {#cell-fig-routing .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} flagged = sorted(book, key=lambda r: r["tail"], reverse=True)[:12] top = flagged[::-1] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.8, 4.2)) colors = [COOL if r["same_sector"] else CRASH for r in top] ax.barh([r["pair"] for r in top], [r["tail"] for r in top], color=colors) ax.set_xlabel("Pearson − Spearman (heavy-joint-tail score)") ax.set_title("The measure book → routing queue", fontsize=12) annotate_box(ax, 0.62, 0.20, "cross-sector → Job C\n(illusory diversification)", va="bottom", fontsize=9) despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The finished measure book as a routing chart. Each bar is a pair's Pearson − Spearman gap — the heavy-joint-tail score — for the twelve heaviest tails. Cross-sector pairs (red) dominate the top: the diversification illusions that couple only in the tail, routed to Job C. The strongly-coupled within-sector pairs (blue) carry a smaller gap and, with their clean four-lens agreement, route to Job A for calibration.
